name: How to Prepare for a Tub-to-Shower Conversion Consultation

step.name: Step 1: Document the Existing Bathroom
step.text: Measure the bathroom and tub area, including wall-to-wall dimensions, ceiling height, doorway width, drain position, and the locations of valves, supply lines, outlets, lights, and the exhaust fan. Take clear photos of the tub surround, adjacent walls, floor, ceiling, and any signs of staining or movement. Note the home’s age if known and disclose previous leaks, repairs, plumbing problems, or renovations. Done means the contractor has enough information to discuss likely layout options before an in-person inspection.

step.name: Step 2: Define How the Shower Must Work
step.text: Write down who will use the shower and what would make entry, bathing, cleaning, and storage easier. Decide whether you want a standard curb, low threshold, or curbless approach, plus features such as a handheld sprayer, seat, grab bars, recessed niche, or larger controls. Do not select features based only on appearance. A curbless design may require careful work at the drain and floor structure, while a seat or future grab bars may require planned support behind finished surfaces.

step.name: Step 3: Choose the Layout and Materials
step.text: Ask the design-build team to compare keeping the existing footprint with relocating the drain, controls, or other fixtures. Keeping plumbing close to its current location may simplify the scope, while relocation can improve usability but may affect flooring, walls, framing, and cost. Bring preferred examples of shower walls, tile, glass, trim, fixtures, and flooring. Confirm who supplies each item, whether installation products are included, and which selections must be finalized before construction begins.

step.name: Step 4: Confirm Permits and Technical Work
step.text: Ask which portions require building, plumbing, electrical, or mechanical permits in the property’s jurisdiction. San Diego County guidance says regulated alterations to building systems require the required permit before work begins; cities may have their own procedures and review requirements. Confirm how the plan addresses waterproofing, shower ventilation, lighting, GFCI protection, water-conserving fixtures where applicable, and inspection scheduling. A complete answer should identify responsibility rather than leaving permit tasks unclear.

step.name: Step 5: Review the Written Proposal
step.text: Compare proposals by scope, not just the total figure. Look for demolition and disposal, surface preparation, plumbing, electrical, ventilation, waterproofing, finish installation, glass, painting, permits, inspections, cleanup, exclusions, allowances, and change-order procedures. Ask how concealed damage is handled after demolition. The proposal should explain how additional work is priced and approved, especially for deteriorated framing, subfloor damage, outdated plumbing, or unexpected drain conditions.

step.name: Step 6: Plan for Construction and Inspection
step.text: Before demolition, remove personal items, protect belongings, and establish how the bathroom will be accessed. Ask when water may be shut off, how dust and debris will be controlled, and how the work area will be separated from the rest of the home. The project is not complete merely because the shower looks finished. Confirm that required inspections have occurred, fixtures operate correctly, water drains properly, sealant and grout are complete, and cleanup responsibilities are satisfied.

step.name: Step 7: Schedule the Design Consultation
step.text: Give the remodeling team your measurements, photos, priority list, preferred materials, and questions. Elite Remodeling & Design, Inc. describes a process that can include consultation, design development, 3D visualization, material selections, permitting coordination, construction, and final inspection. Use the meeting to test whether the proposed shower fits the household’s needs and the home’s existing conditions. A useful next step is a site evaluation followed by a written scope that separates confirmed work from allowances or items requiring further investigation. Key Takeaways Gather dimensions, photos, repair history, and user needs before the first meeting. Decide which access features are essential rather than treating them as late additions. Compare written scopes and allowances, not totals alone. Confirm local permit, inspection, waterproofing, ventilation, and electrical responsibilities. Contact Elite Remodeling & Design, Inc. with the bathroom details and conversion goals to begin planning.
